Craps Buy and Lay Bets: The Vig You Pay for True Odds

Published October 30, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Our craps place bets guide covers the most common way to bet directly on a number repeating before a 7 — but place bets quietly shortchange you on two of the six numbers, paying less than the true mathematical odds would suggest. Buy and Lay bets exist specifically to close that gap. They pay the real odds instead of the house's rounded-down place-bet payout, but the casino doesn't give that up for free: it charges a commission, usually called the vig, for the privilege. Whether that trade is worth making depends entirely on which number you're betting and how the specific casino charges the fee, and the math is clean enough to work through in full.

How a Buy bet works

A Buy bet is a wager that one specific number — 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, or 10 — rolls again before a 7 shows, exactly like a Place bet. The difference is what it pays. A Place bet pays a fixed house-set ratio (9-to-5 on 4 or 10, 7-to-5 on 5 or 9, 7-to-6 on 6 or 8) that's deliberately rounded in the house's favor. A Buy bet instead pays the true odds of that number repeating before a 7: exactly 2-to-1 on 4 or 10, exactly 3-to-2 on 5 or 9, exactly 6-to-5 on 6 or 8. In exchange for that better payout, the casino charges a commission — typically 5% of the amount you're betting, often with a $1 minimum regardless of bet size, which is why Buy bets are usually made in amounts like $20 or $25 rather than oddly-sized numbers that would make the 5% calculation awkward.

How a Lay bet works

A Lay bet is the mirror image: you're betting that a 7 rolls before a specific number repeats. Because a 7 is more likely than any individual point number, laying a number means risking more to win less — you're the one holding the favorite's side of the bet. The payout follows the same true-odds logic as a Buy bet, just inverted: laying 4 or 10 pays 1-to-2, laying 5 or 9 pays 2-to-3, laying 6 or 8 pays 5-to-6. The commission on a Lay bet is also 5%, but it's charged on the win amount — the smaller side of the payout — rather than on the amount risked, since the amount risked on a Lay bet is already larger than the potential win.

The detail that trips up new players: on a Buy bet, the 5% commission is calculated on your wager. On a Lay bet, it's calculated on your potential winnings, not on the (larger) amount you're risking. Mixing those two up is the single most common mistake in figuring out whether a Lay bet is actually worth making at a given price.

The commission: how it's charged, and why that detail matters

There's a second variable that changes the real math more than most players realize: when the commission is actually collected. Some casinos charge the vig upfront, the moment you make the bet, win or lose. Others only charge it if the bet wins, often called "win-only" or "vig on win" commission. Those two policies produce meaningfully different house edges on the exact same bet, because paying the fee every time you bet is a steadily bigger drag than paying it only on the fraction of bets that actually win.

A Buy 4 or Buy 10 with commission charged every time works out to a house edge of about 1.67% — genuinely one of the best bets on the entire craps table, rivaling pass-line odds. The same bet with commission charged only on wins carries a house edge closer to 4.76%, which is a real difference even though it's the identical bet on the identical number. Since house rules on this vary by casino and aren't always posted obviously at the table, it's a fair, normal question to ask a dealer before you commit to Buy and Lay bets as a regular part of your strategy.

Why Buy bets only make sense on 4 and 10

Here's the part that catches a lot of players off guard: Buy bets are a clearly better deal than Place bets on 4 and 10, roughly break-even on 5 and 9, and actually worse than Place bets on 6 and 8. The reason is that the gap between a Place bet's rounded-down payout and the true odds isn't the same size on every number — it's largest on 4 and 10, where the house's 9-to-5 place payout sits noticeably below the true 2-to-1, and smallest on 6 and 8, where the 7-to-6 place payout already sits close to the true 6-to-5. Paying a flat 5% commission to close a big gap (on 4/10) is a good trade. Paying that same 5% to close an already-small gap (on 6/8) isn't — you end up handing over more in commission than you gain from the better payout.

That's why experienced craps players who use Buy bets at all tend to use them almost exclusively on 4 and 10, and simply Place the 5, 6, 8, and 9 instead.

Lay bets: the mirror image, mostly on 4 and 10 too

The same logic plays out for Lay bets, just flipped. Laying 4 or 10 — betting on the 7 against the two hardest-to-make point numbers — carries a house edge of roughly 2.44%, a solid rate for a bet against the shooter. Laying 6 or 8 runs closer to 4%, and laying 5 or 9 sits in between, which again means the best version of this bet is concentrated on the numbers where the gap between true odds and the standard payout structure is largest. Lay bets see far less action at most tables than Buy bets simply because betting against the shooter feels less natural to most players at a social game built around cheering a hot roll, not because the math is worse.

Place vs. Buy vs. Lay, side by side

NumberPlace bet paysPlace house edgeBuy bet paysBuy house edge (vig always charged)
4 or 109 to 56.67%2 to 1~1.67%
5 or 97 to 54.00%3 to 2~3.23%
6 or 87 to 61.52%6 to 5~4.44%

Read across the 4/10 row and the case for Buy bets is obvious: the house edge roughly drops by two-thirds for the price of a small flat commission. Read across the 6/8 row and it flips — the Place bet already carries one of the lowest house edges on the entire table, and adding a Buy commission on top of true odds actually makes the number worse to bet, not better.

Finding the bet, and what to ask the dealer

Not every casino spreads Buy and Lay bets at every table, and where they're offered, minimum bet sizes for Buy and Lay wagers are often set higher than the table's standard minimum, specifically because of how awkward the 5% commission math gets on small, odd-numbered bets. To place one, you generally hand your chips to the dealer rather than placing them in the come area yourself, and say which number and which bet type you want — the box person will mark your bet and collect or note the commission according to that casino's specific policy. If you're going to make Buy and Lay bets a regular part of how you play craps, the two questions worth asking before you start are simple: is the vig charged every time or only on a win, and is this casino's commission rate the standard 5%. Both answers change the real math enough to matter.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Buy bet always better than a Place bet on the same number?

No. It's clearly better on 4 and 10, roughly a wash on 5 and 9, and worse than Place on 6 and 8, because the commission can end up costing more than the improved payout is worth on numbers where the Place payout was already close to true odds.

Do I pay the commission even if my Buy bet loses?

It depends on the casino. Some charge the 5% vig upfront regardless of outcome, which is the better version of the bet mathematically; others only charge it if the bet wins, which raises the effective house edge. Ask the dealer which policy a specific table uses.

Why is the commission on a Lay bet calculated differently from a Buy bet?

On a Lay bet you're risking more than you stand to win, since you're betting on the more likely outcome (a 7). Casinos calculate the 5% commission on the smaller win amount rather than the larger risk amount, which keeps the fee proportional to what you'd actually collect.

Can I make a Buy or Lay bet at any point during a shooter's roll?

Yes — unlike some craps wagers that are restricted to the come-out roll, Buy and Lay bets on the point numbers can typically be made or removed at any time while a shooter is still rolling, which is one reason experienced players use them as a flexible supplement to Pass Line odds.

Is a Lay bet the same thing as betting against the shooter on the Don't Pass line?

They're related but not identical. A Don't Pass bet is a single wager made before the point is established and tied to the come-out roll, while a Lay bet is made after a point is set and targets one specific number rather than the whole Don't Pass sequence.
